entries.title: German spy scandal threatens national security
entries.summary: The arrest of Germany's former intelligence chief August Hanning could undermine national security, experts warn, as allies may reconsider their intelligence relationships.
entries.content:
Germany

German spy scandal threatens national security

October 7, 2026

The arrest of Germany's former intelligence chief August Hanning could undermine national security, experts warn, as allies may reconsider their intelligence relationships.

The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D.*, is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

Manfred D. is accused of having sold around 2,000 highly classified documents to Hanning over a period of 12 years, long after the latter stepped down from the BND in 2005, after seven years as its chief. Manfred D. continued to serve all of Hanning's successors, including the current BND chief Martin Jäger, before retiring in March this year.

On one occasion, the state prosecutor said, Hanning "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."

According to Florian Flade, reporter for public broadcaster ARD, most of these documents were weekly intelligence briefings delivered to the German government by the BND, including the latest findings from partner intelligence agencies in other countries.

"This is very, very sensitive because it involves partner agencies in other countries," Flade told DW's Berlin Briefing podcast. "And we heard this also involves information about the Iranian nuclear program, the Russian military, also the Ukraine war."

Broken trust, broken credibility

Some pundits now say that the biggest concern is what conclusions the intelligence agencies of allied countries will draw from this affair. In the past, the US CIA is known to have shared information on radical Islamists in Germany, which possibly helped to prevent terrorist attacks in the country.

If it now emerges that information was leaving the BND via Hanning, that relationship could be undermined, particularly if it was also eventually ending up in the hands of the intelligence agencies of Russia and China (though there is no suggestion of that as yet).

"There's huge damage being done not only to the outer appearance and image of the BND," said Flade. "There's a damage assessment now happening within the BND. Also, they're talking to partners about this because they want to know if their information was given to other countries."

That could also potentially have consequences for Germany's national security in the growing confrontation with Russia. The BND, which is currently subject to more legal restrictions than other intelligence agencies around the world, considers its relationship with its US counterpart as vital.

"There might be a change in the amount of information that is coming from the US and others," Flade added, though ultimately, he pointed out, it might be difficult for the BND to know what they're not being told.

Only a day before the scandal broke, current BND President Martin Jäger reiterated his concern that Germany could slide into a military conflict with Russia, telling a parliamentary hearing that the Kremlin was already waging a "shadow war," and that further military rearmament was "unfortunately necessary" —  though he did say that there was currently no indication of active preparations from Russia.

Flade said that, behind the scenes, Jäger is furious about the leak of information from Manfred D., and called a meeting on Tuesday of all BND officials to underline the how serious the consequences of sharing information could be. New internal security measures are also being put in place.

The new case could not have come at a worse time for Jäger or the BND. For one thing, new laws are currently being prepared to expand the agency's powers, partly to improve the BND's standing among its foreign partners.

For another thing, another BND agent, Carsten L. and a businessman named Arthur E., are currently on trial in Berlin on treason charges for passing on classified documents to the Russian secret service in 2022.

New rules for old officials?

The case has also raised questions about what former intelligence officials should and shouldn't be allowed to do once they leave office. Hanning founded his own security consultancy business after he left the BND, for which he apparently used his contacts and knowledge to advise his clients. This is legal and tolerated, but many think it shouldn't be.

Timo Lange, of the NGO LobbyControl, said that the Hanning case shows why former intelligence officials must be prevented from working as security consultants in any capacity for the rest of their lives.

"It is fundamentally problematic when high-ranking officials from the intelligence or military sectors, after leaving government service, act as consultants for various — and in some cases unknown — clients from abroad," Lange said in a statement. "This is an obvious gateway for illegitimate foreign influence and jeopardizes the security interests of Germany and the European Union."

But as Flade pointed out, Hanning's career path is not exactly unusual. "These people are trying to just make some money with what they can do best, which is networking and then selling the security assessments that they do," he said. "And yeah, working for companies or even for other countries as a consultant."

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

entries.title: France suspends use of stun grenades against protesters
entries.summary: France is suspending the use of stun grenades against protesters as allegations of student brutality draw more anger. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is also set to address the nation later this evening.
entries.content:
France

France suspends use of stun grenades against protesters

October 7, 2026

France is suspending the use of stun grenades against protesters as allegations of student brutality draw more anger. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is also set to address the nation later this evening.

France is suspending the use of stun grenades at student-led protests as people report allegations of police brutality at demonstrations that have widened over the weeks.

"I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL radio broadcaster on Wednesday.

He emphasized that the suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened."

Nunez announced the measure to curb growing anger after reports about teenagers having lost their hands or teeth during protests drew anger.

French regional newspaper La Voix du Nord reported this Monday that a 15-year-old had his hand and a part of his lower arm blown off after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated during protests.

Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the jaw as a tear gas canister was fired during protests, with the officer having been charged on Tuesday.

The order also comes before an address by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to protesters later Wednesday evening.

More to follow.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges
entries.summary: August Hanning has been remanded into pretrial detention after his arrest. The case has prompted calls for transparency when spies leave the government.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention

October 7, 2026

August Hanning has been remanded into pretrial detention after his arrest. The case has prompted calls for transparency when spies leave the government.

Former German foreign intelligence agency boss August Hanning appeared before a federal judge in the western city of Karlsruhe on Wednesday following his arrest on espionage and treason charges Tuesday.

He has been ordered to remain in detention ahead of his trial, according to federal prosecutors.

Manfred D., Hanning's former chief of staff at the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), was also detained.

What are the charges against Hanning?

Manfred D. is accused of having stolen secret documents and turned these over to Hanning, who, as a private-sector security adviser, in turn reportedly sold the secret documents to an as yet unnamed foreign spy agency or agencies.

Investigators estimate the two stole and potentially passed on more than 2,000 secret documents between 2010 and 2023. Federal investigators say it is unclear how much information was stolen and to whom it was sold.

Hanning ran the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 until 2005 before becoming state secretary at the Federal Interior Ministry and then entering private business as a security adviser.

The issue has raised serious questions about the trustworthiness of Germany's intelligence agencies and shocked politicians into action as they claim not enough is being done to ensure high-ranking officials do not abuse their experience when transitioning to jobs in the private sector.

Who was Hanning selling data to?

Although it is currently not known who Hanning's potential customers were, Germany's weekly Der Spiegel magazine on Wednesday named Azerbaijan as one. The Azerbaijan Media and Broadcasting Council vehemently denied the accusation, calling it "unfounded" and adding, "The malicious intent of the ‌forces behind this disinformation operation is ‌to ​damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations."

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?
entries.summary: Lawmakers of the center-right CDU may have voted for the far-right AfD candidate for parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt. Germany's Social Democrats warn of a "unique breach of taboos."
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Did CDU lawmakers support the far-right AfD?

October 7, 2026

Lawmakers of the center-right CDU may have voted for the far-right AfD candidate for parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt. Germany's Social Democrats warn of a "unique breach of taboos."

Following events in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, speculation is rife that lawmakers from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) helped elect a far-right extremist as parliamentary speaker.

This would not only violate prior internal agreements, but also come despite the insistence of CDU Chairman, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, that his party would not cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) anywhere.

In the first session of the parliament in Magdeburg, the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, following the AfD's election victory on September 6, Tobias Rausch was elected parliamentary speaker — the first time a representative of a far-right party had held such a position since the end of World War II. 

Rausch was backed by his own party and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Rationality (BSW), formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, as had been expected.  However, he also received four additional votes by secret ballot. Most observers believe these votes could only have come from right-wing CDU lawmakers.

Leading members of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) were quick to take to the streets in protest in Berlin on Tuesday, marching from the Bundestag through the Brandenburg Gate to nearby Bebelplatz — the very spot where, in 1933, the Nazis burned books by authors they deemed unacceptable. The march concluded with SPD Federal Minister of Defense Boris Pistorius leading the crowd in the German national anthem. Many participants displayed copies of the German Basic Law, a symbol of democracy to stand up for the rule of law and the constitution.

Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) summarized the situation, "Electing far-right extremists to such an office represents a taboo brake. Not only the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could have happened." Klingbeil's SPD is, after all, the junior coalition partner in the federal government.

The events in Magdeburg thus also cast a shadow over the governing coalition.

Did the AfD receive votes from the CDU?

It didn't help much that the leader of the CDU parliamentary group, Thorsten Frei, was careful in his wording.

"It's a secret ballot, so of course, in principle, anybody is suspect." he said. He also added, "The fact that this happened is, in my view, extremely troubling and cause for concern."

The result of the first election in the new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt thus offers only a glimpse of the fierce debates to come on how to deal with the AfD. The far-right party won 44% of the vote after having campaigned on extremely tough immigration policies, climate change denial and calls for the near-total abolition of public broadcasting.

Despite its election victory, the AfD does not have a parliamentary majority on its own. In the small eastern state, the regional branch of the party has been classified by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

Will CDU politicians help elect an AfD state premier into office?

So once again, the debate about the "firewall" returns. The term refers to the stance taken by democratic parties of ruling out any form of cooperation with the AfD.

At the city and municipal levels, this approach has long since stopped working. Many political analysts have pointed out that the "firewall" has not benefited the CDU, but cooperating with the AfD is also seen as a slippery slope.

Georg Maier, the SPD Interior Minister of the state of Thuringia, agrees. "If the CDU continues down this path, it will contribute to its own downfall. The firewall does serve a purpose."

BSW co-leader Fabio De Masi told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper, "We have to pull the AfD out from behind the firewall. Until now, it hasn't had to prove anything and has been able to conceal its internal contradictions. I don't want the AfD to continue growing behind the firewall."

The BSW, a party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht that has retained some left-wing positions while also aligning itself with the AfD on social issues, paved the way for Rausch's election as parliamentary speaker when it announced that it would vote for him.

The BSW barely managed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. How closely its five MPs want to work with the AfD in the future remains to be seen.

AfD caucus leader Oliver Kirchner recently expressed criticism of BSW co-leaders De Masi and Mohamed Ali, who both have an immigrant background.

"Am I now supposed to spend five years in politics with people who are under the leadership of Mohamed Ali and this half-Italian guy who says, 'They're all Nazis'?" Kirchner told the right-wing magazine Compact earlier this month.

Up until now, support from the BSW has been seen as the AfD's only real chance of coming to power in Saxony-Anhalt. The other parties — the CDU, the SPD, the Greens and the Left Party — continue to categorically rule out any cooperation with the AfD. Whether that will remain the case in the coming weeks is now the big question.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai
entries.summary: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to Henri B. Kagan, Kenso Soai

October 7, 2026

Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their groundbreaking discoveries related to the origin of chirality and life's building blocks.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry on Wednesday was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Kagan, who is 95 years old and was born in France, is affiliated with France’s Université Paris-Sud, and Soai, who is 76 years old and was born in Japan, is based at the Tokyo University of Science.

The scientists share the Nobel Prize for answering longstanding questions in chemistry about life's origins.

Specifically, the duo solved an age-old mystery that has long puzzled chemists: some molecules, like amino acids, exist as two variants that are mirror images of one another, but just one of the variants out of the two is found in living organisms.

The two answered questions about why life chooses one variant over another.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

Nobel chemistry prize goes to scientists who answered questions about homochirality

In chemistry, life's building blocks are what scientists call homochiral, after the Greek words for "same" and "hand."

The Nobel Committee said the chemistry prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

Who won the Nobel chemistry prize last year?

Last year, Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside. Their discoveries can help tackle some of the world's most pressing problems, like climate change.

What do laureates receive?

  • Laureates receive a tailored diploma, a medal and a document detailing the cash award that is set this year to 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.

Who else has received a Nobel Prize so far?

  • The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work on optogenetics, a method of controlling nerve cells with light, which makes it possible to study how the brain works.
  • The Nobel Prize in physics was awarded Tuesday to Francis Halzen, a Belgian-born astrophysicist whose efforts helped demistify a rare group of neutrinos that launched a new era of astronomy.

Nobel prizes in literature and peace also this week

  • The Nobel Prize in literature is set to be awarded Thursday and the Nobel peace prize will be announced on Friday.
  • After that, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.
  • All prize announcements are streamed live by the Nobel Prize organization.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
entries.summary: After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.
entries.content:
Published October 5, 2026last updated October 7, 2026

After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had caused the death.

UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."

What you need to know about plague

  • There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
  • The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
  • Bubonic plague is the most common form; it does not spread from person to person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure.
  • If the bacteria reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is highly contagious because it can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing.
  • If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.

Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.

She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."

Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection

All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.

The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.

Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.

A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.

What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?

Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

All are caused by the same bacterium.

What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.

Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours

Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.

Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.

Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.

The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Ronaldo stays on under cloud as Messi exits internationals
entries.summary: Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.
entries.content:
Portugal

Recapping Ronaldo and Messi's eventful, contrasting Tuesday

October 7, 2026

Just hours before Lionel Messi played his last match for Argentina, Cristiano Ronaldo posted his latest salvo in a row with Portugal. Ronaldo wants to play on despite the troubles, while Messi bathed in adulation.

They are the two players who have defined the last two decades. As football became ever more popular, commercial and dominant in the cultural and sporting landscape, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi remained its twin peaks.

Along with that has come endless social media posts, stories and discussions about who is better. Does Messi's World Cup and two Copa America titles with Argentina trump Ronaldo's Euro 2016 win and two Nations League titles? Or does the Portuguese's greater number of goals mean more? How about their club honors?

It is, essentially, a subjective argument and not one that can ever be resolved. It remains to be seen whether that's also true of the public spat between Ronaldo and his Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

On Tuesday, Messi scored a 126th goal in his 208th game for Argentina. Shortly before he did, Ronaldo posted a 2,000-word statement in which he stopped short of quitting the national team but said there was an "absolute breakdown of trust" between him and the coach.

'There will be time' for Ronaldo's Portugal farewell

Ronaldo's comments refer to Portugal's recent match against Norway in which he said he was initially to be rested before being asked to warm up as a substitute without ever being brought on. The striker, 41, walked away from the team's camp for the remainder of the international break, but said the story is not over.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," said Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

"Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach's word, as anyone who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it," Ronaldo said. "The responsibility is entirely mine. I apologize to the Portuguese people once again, but the breaking of one's word has, for me, a defining impact.

"I felt that, from that point on, my staying would only harm the group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I didn't feel useful: I picked up my bags and left," he continued before suggesting he accepted there may be a need for the coach or federation to punish him.

Messi: Argentina exit 'deeply painful'

It was a long way from the emotional scenes in Rosario, Argentina. Instead of anger and recrimination, the overriding emotions there were gratitude, nostalgia and sadness.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you," Messi, who now plays his club football for Inter Miami in the US, told the 80,000 fans who had packed in to see him score a penalty in a 3-0 win over Benin.

For some, the contrasting evenings offered a neat synopsis of the pair. Ronaldo, less naturally gifted than his counterpart, has made the most of his talents with a singular focus which many believe often makes him prioritize himself over the team. He has had similar fallouts with managers and head coaches before, including Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, Erik ten Hag at Manchester United and Portugal's 2022 World Cup coach, Fernando Santos.

Ronaldo has 100 goals in his sights

Ronaldo's much-discussed aim to reach 1,000 career goals is held up by some as further evidence of where his motivations lie.

"You know what my goal is. I want to win trophies, and I want to reach that number (1,000 goals) that you all know. I will reach the number for sure, if no injuries," he said last December. He is currently on 979.

For others, that is simply what is required to be the best. While Messi's quiet character and general refusal to play out his life in public suggest a more humble character focused on helping the team, his genius has undoubtedly changed the teams around him. In the 2026 World Cup, he barely broke into a run but still led an otherwise fairly limited Argentina to the final with eight goals.

There will be no more Messi goals for Argentina and, despite his promises, no absolute assurances that the world will see Ronaldo in a Portugal shirt again. For now, both will head back to their club sides to play out their twilight years away from the intensity of Europe's top leagues. But wherever they go from here, the spotlight will keep following.

Edited by: Davis VanOpdorp

entries.title: Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur
entries.summary: After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur

October 7, 2026

After being chosen for one of the world's most prestigious awards, some Nobel laureates lose touch with reality and suddenly start spouting unscientific nonsense. They're afflicted by what some have called "Nobelitis."

Linus Pauling won not one, but two Nobel Prizes — the first, for chemistry, in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond, and the Peace Prize in 1962 for his work in the anti-nuclear weapons movement.

The American chemist not only won two Nobel Prizes, but won them on his own, a rare feat for any scientist. Such an honor often turns laureates into global superstars overnight, with millions hanging on their every word.

Nobel laureates can fall victim to Nobelitis

That instant fame can be dangerous, said Nils Hansson, a professor in the Department of History, Theory and Ethics of Medicine at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. Especially, he said, when these world-renowned experts "start spreading crazy, unproven scientific theories" — ideas that, when disseminated by Nobel laureates, risk being taken seriously.

That's what happened with Pauling. Beginning in the mid 1960s he began claiming that vitamin C was a universal remedy, a cure for everything from cancer to cardiovascular conditions and degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis or osteoarthritis.

Pauling developed an alternative treatment he called orthomolecular medicine, based on specific doses of vitamins and minerals for each patient. To this day, some 60 years later, evidence for his methods remains inconclusive.

Pauling's case is a classic example of "Nobelitis," or "Nobel disease" — not an official diagnosis, but an informal term used to describe how some laureates begin to suffer delusions of grandeur later in life. It was first coined by Paul Nurse, president of The Royal Society, the UK's national academy of sciences, and himself a winner of the Nobel Prize.

'Be skeptical of everything'

"Be skeptical of everything, including yourself and your own ideas," Nurse said in a 2019 interview with KU Leuven University in Belgium, when asked what made someone a good scientist. In cases of Nobelitis, that self-skepticism is the first to go.

That was also the case with virologist Luc Montagnier, who was jointly honored in 2008 for his discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, with colleague Francoise Barre-Sinoussi in the early 1980s.

Montagnier would later go on to support homeopathic medicine, another alternative treatment of disease and claim that HIV transmission in Africa could be diminished through better hygiene and nutrition.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier said the SARS-CoV-2 virus had been created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code. "It's difficult for a practicing virologist to say that a Nobel laureate in virology is spreading nonsense," said German virologist Christian Drosten on NDR's Coronavirus Update podcast in May 2020. "But that is utter nonsense."

James Watson, who was never known for his modesty, also let fame go to his head. In 1962, he was awarded the Nobel Prize along with Maurice Wilkins and Francis Crick for their discovery of the structure of the DNA molecule. But in the early 2000s, Watson repeatedly spread racist theories that Black people were less intelligent than white people.

For medical historian Hansson, Watson is a prime example that the Nobel Prize is not automatically awarded to a person who should be considered as a role model.

"You may have made a fantastic discovery, but that doesn't make you a universal genius," he said.

Even Noble Prize winners need to be challenged

But the great expectations of an admiring public may also contribute to the development of Nobelitis. Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine in 2001, soon found himself getting daily requests for interviews on all sorts of topics.

"As if suddenly I was acknowledgeable about all workings of the world and of human beings," he told DW.

Nurse had this advice for researchers: "Be careful quite what you say. Talk about things that you do know something about that would be fine. And if you don't know so much or you're not sure about something, be really clear that you're not sure."

Hansson has also noticed that the media eagerly report whatever Nobel laureates say — even when prize winners stray far from their area of expertise.

Nobelitis sufferers are leaders in their fields, and rightly honored for their work with the Nobel. But they're also regular individuals, not immune to megalomania and other behavioral problems — meaning that homeopathy, orthomolecular medicine and other pseudosciences don't automatically become credible just because they're backed by a Nobel Prize winner.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: The solar boom is rapidly transforming emerging economies
entries.summary: Renewable electricity is cheaper than ever. So while the West got rich on coal and oil, some of the poorest countries in the world are banking on solar, wind and water instead.
entries.content:
October 7, 2026

Renewable electricity is cheaper than ever. So while the West got rich on coal and oil, some of the poorest countries in the world are banking on solar, wind and water instead.

As emerging economies and global standards of living grow, is the world in for another fossil fuel boom? The data says not. Countries from Southeast Asia to Sub-Saharan Africa aren't investing in fossil fuels like the West did, but in electricity, powered by renewables.

When the US and Europe industrialized in the 19th and 20th century, they did so using fossil energy. From coal ovens, gas heating and combustion engine cars to electricity produced in coal and gas power plants, entire societies relied on polluting sources of fuel.

Yet while burning fossil fuels allowed industrialized countries to boom, it also caused the climate crisis that is linked to extreme weather events around the world today.

Renewable electricity is rapidly becoming the cheapest option

Many of the same countries that became economically powerful off the back of fossil fuels are now trying to transition to renewables. But they are held back by centuries of legacy infrastructure.

Because a gas boiler won't run on wind power, and a diesel truck cannot be solar-powered, societies looking to shift to green energy need to use more electricity and increase their share of renewables.

That is where many middle- and lower-income countries have an advantage. With less existing energy infrastructure built around fossil fuels, they are better placed for a faster rollout of renewable electricity sources. 

In many instances, solar power in particular is now cheaper to produce than fossil electricity. And unlike large coal or gas plants, which take years to construct and millions in investments, solar and wind farms can be built quickly and with much less upfront cost.

At the same time, according to an analysis by renewables think tank Ember, electronic devices like refrigerators, electric stoves or air conditioners have all become much cheaper in the last decades, making electricity a more affordable option as an energy source for cooking, heating and more.  

While electric cars are still a luxury item in most places, their prices are coming down too. And a UN study found that in India, Indonesia and Vietnam electric scooters and motorbikes already cost the same as petrol models. Yet a lot less to fuel.

All this means that renewable electricity is quickly becoming the best choice for the wallet — not just for the climate. And countries are taking note.

"We're seeing a leapfrog take place right across the emerging markets,” said Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist at Ember. "The whole of Asia is electrifying quickly, and the whole of Europe and the United States is stagnant."

Lower-income countries are electrifying faster

In 2023, only around a quarter of global electricity was generated by renewables. But that figure is rising fast, and almost all new capacity added these days is based on solar or wind power. 

Lower-income countries already use less fossil fuels and more renewables than higher-income ones.

And large middle-income economies are outpacing richer ones as well. In 2023, solar power alone made up at least six percent and ten percent of electricity in India and Vietnam respectively. The global average was five percent.

Lower-income countries are electrifying without the fossil detour

This boom has meant middle- and lower income countries are electrifying fast, consuming less energy directly from fossil fuels than richer countries. Vietnam, for instance, is already using more electric energy than the US, Europe and even China, and India is following the same path.

But the potential for energy leapfrogging might be particularly high in low-income countries, most of them across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia or Namibia are expanding their energy infrastructure rapidly right now to meet the demands of a growing, young population. But rural areas in many countries are not connected to electricity grids. 

And Joel Nana, project manager at South African NGO Sustainable Energy Africa says that "even when there is access to power, it's often not reliable.”

Until a few years ago, he says, people would default to diesel generators to fill their energy needs. But that came at a cost, because importing fuel is particularly expensive in many African countries, meaning energy crises and oil price fluctuations hit much harder.

Renewables for energy access and independence

These factors make solar power a solution for both energy access and independence. And it has become so cheap that Nana says it's a "no brainer”.

"Some businesses can make back their investment in just two years, so why would you want to deploy anything else?” he said. "Solar has rapidly become the de facto default technology that everyone falls back on.”

And once it is set up, it is very effective. Sub-Saharan Africa is extremely well-suited to solar power. It gets more sun than almost anywhere in the world, and has enough space for solar farms to cover electricity demand hundreds of times over.  

"If you add solar plus batteries, you can get cheap electricity about 90 percent of the time from the sun alone”, said Kingsmill Bond.

Countries like Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Senegal have expanded their solar capacity massively in the past few years.

In a 2026 report for African Tech Futures Lab and Ember, Nana analyzed import data from China and estimated that around 100,000 solar panels were installed across Africa every day in 2026, up 45 percent from just the previous year.

Similar trends are emerging all across the world. In Pakistan, for example, people have been buying solar panels from China en masse in the past few years to avoid steep electricity grid prices and frequent power outages.

Cheap energy boosts economies

Aleksi Lumijärvi, director for knowledge, policy and finance at the International Renewable Energy Association says these decisions can have a major impact on the global economy in the coming decades.

"Industrial companies will find that it will be cheaper to move production to, for example, somewhere in Sub-Saharan Africa, because they have this cheap, clean solar power plus batteries available.”

Kingsmill Bond says where electricity is cheap and abundant, wealth will follow.

"You're going to have faster growth in the emerging markets, you will have fewer financial crises. It will make a material difference to people's quality of lives.”

Nana says the next step for African countries is to establish policies that ensure everyone benefits from the solar boom.

"We are heading towards the most decentralized grid in the whole world within the next five years,” he told DW. His mantra for governments, he says, is: "This is happening, whether you like it or not.” He expects a wave of new energy regulations, many of which are now in the final stages of negotiation, to come into effect across Africa in the coming months and years.

"Countries are realizing it's in their interest to integrate this technology into national strategies, to share the benefits and to make use of this competitive advantage.”

Edited by: Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün

All data and code behind this analysis can be found in this Github repository.

More data-driven stories by DW can be found here.

entries.title: Israel marks third anniversary of October 7 Hamas terror attacks with memorials
entries.summary: Families gathered at the Nova music festival site and other attack locations in memory of those killed by Hamas on October 7, 2023.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel marks third anniversary of October 7 terror attacks

October 7, 2026

Families gathered at the Nova music festival site and other attack locations in memory of those killed by Hamas on October 7, 2023.

Israel is marking the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attack on Wednesday with memorials across the country.

At the site of the Nova music festival, where more than 300 people were killed, families gathered at dawn for a moment of silence and paid tribute in front of portraits both of festival-goers and security forces who died on October 7.

At the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another attack site, mourners watched in silence the raising of an Israeli flag.

Others are expected to gather at intersections and bomb shelters to mark one of the deadliest attacks against Israel, which killed more than 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage.

The last living hostages were released a year ago under a US-brokered ceasefire deal.

The anniversary of the attacks also comes just ahead of the October 27 elections in Israel.

Germany stands firmly by Israel's side, says Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday reaffirmed Germany's support for Israel on the anniversary, saying the country stood firmly by Israel's side and was committed to preventing a repeat of the October 7 attack.

"We stand for the security and existence of Israel," the German chancellor said.

Merz also called for a political settlement saying for peace and security in the region "can best be achieved through the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel."

Warning of rising antisemitism in Germany, Merz said his government would "do everything in its power to consistently combat antisemitism in all its new and old forms."

Two dead in Gaza in Israeli strikes

New Israeli strikes in Gaza on Wednesday killed two people, Palestinian officials reported.

One of those killed was identified as a volunteer with the emergency rescue agency under Hamas. The European Union, as well as the United States, Germany, and other countries, classify Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Israel's war in Gaza following the October 7 attacks has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the territory's Health Ministry, around half of them women and children, and displaced most of the population.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher
